details: Human touch sensation is subjective, relative, and deceptive.
Touch judgment depends on the prior thermal state of skin rather than absolute object temperature.
Objective scientific measurement requires calibrated quantitative instruments (thermometers).
Inconsistent touch feedback necessitates standardized thermometric temperature scales.

details: Temperature: Quantitative measure of the degree of hotness or coldness of a body. Standard Unit: Degree Celsius (°C).
Clinical Thermometer: Designed specifically for human body temperature (scale range: 35°C to 42°C; normal human body temp = 37.0°C / 98.6°F). Features a capillary kink/constriction.
Kink/Constriction Function: Prevents mercury column from dropping back automatically when removed from patient's mouth.
Digital Thermometer: Modern electronic instrument using heat sensors, eliminating toxic mercury glass hazards.
Laboratory Thermometer: Designed for experimental liquid temperatures (scale range: -10°C to 110°C). Lacks a kink.

details: Keep thermometer strictly vertical; do not tilt.
Thermometer bulb must be fully submerged in liquid without touching bottom or side walls of beaker.
Line of Sight: Eye must be positioned horizontally inline with top level of liquid column to avoid parallax error.
Laboratory thermometers must be read while bulb remains fully immersed in measured liquid.

details: Maximum-Minimum Thermometer: Specialized meteorological instrument recording daily maximum and minimum atmospheric temperatures.
Meteorological Tracking: Monitoring temperature trends helps predict weather changes and climate patterns.
Historical Pioneer: Anna Mani, pioneering Indian meteorologist who developed indigenous weather instruments and atmospheric research tools.
Atmospheric data collection is critical for agricultural forecasting and disaster preparedness.
